elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Section 15.5 is retained unchanged: "This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York without reference to any rules of conflict of laws." New York is the preferred governing law, so no edit was needed.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.
elements.evidence: Revised 15.6(a) now reads that a Dispute "shall be brought exclusively in the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, and each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of such courts over the merits of any Dispute," and expressly disapplies the arbitral machinery ("Sections 15.6(b) through (e) shall not apply"). The only other-forum route left in the redlined text is 15.6(j), which was narrowed from broad "equitable relief or interim or provisional relief" to "temporary or interim injunctive relief ... temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction," i.e. the customary temporary-injunctive carve-out that does not defeat merits exclusivity. Retained 15.6(h) (patent/trademark validity in the granting country) and 15.6(i) (invention ownership) are pre-existing, jurisdiction-mandated IP mechanics rather than an alternate merits forum for Agreement disputes, and the Section 2.10 JSC / Section 5.6 carve-outs are original internal escalation mechanics, not court/arbitral fora.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause keeps New York law (Section 15.5). This is the preferred position and is superior to the fallback; the fallback level is simply not the level pursued.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: The forum is now the state and federal courts in New York County, not Delaware, California or London. Not a defect \u2014 the preferred level is satisfied instead.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: New York law was already in place and the redline supplies the missing element \u2014 exclusive merits jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County \u2014 in place of JAMS arbitration in a redacted seat.

The original clause did fail both levels: 15.6(a) sent all merits Disputes to mandatory arbitration in an undisclosed ([***]) seat, leaving courts available only to enter judgment on the award, so 'deviation' is the correct finding status.

Narrowing 15.6(j) from 'equitable relief or interim or provisional relief ... or other interim equitable relief' to temporary/interim injunctive relief is necessary, not gratuitous: the broader original wording would have permitted final equitable relief in another forum and defeated the 'subject only to temporary injunctive relief' element.

The conforming edits are within scope and do not add extras: (f) drops only the now-meaningless 'arbitrators are not empowered' limb while preserving the punitive/exemplary damages waiver; (g) preserves the compliance obligation and the stay of termination verbatim except for 'arbitration' \u2192 'proceeding'; the English-language sentence is preserved and conformed. No survival tail, expense allocation, damages category or procedure was added.

Switching off (b)\u2013(e) by an express disapplication sentence rather than deleting them avoids renumbering and leaves no contradiction, since the retained arbitrator-selection text is expressly inoperative; the retained Section 2.10 JSC and Section 5.6 carve-outs and the 15.6(h)/(i) IP mechanics were correctly left intact rather than stripped.

One housekeeping point for the drafter (not a defect on the face of the cited text): confirm no other provision of the Agreement cross-refers to 'the arbitrators', 'the arbitration' or 'the award' under Section 15.6 (e.g. fee-shifting, confidentiality of the proceeding, or a limitation-of-liability reference), so that no dangling arbitration reference survives elsewhere in the document.
